source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: Founding design for the strong-vs-weak cue claim. 24-word lists were studied alone (O), with a weak cue (W) or with a strong cue (S). They were then tested with no cue, a weak cue or a strong cue (3 input x 4 output conditions; the fourth output condition was free recall of cue and target words). Two word lists were used.
numbers: Exp I: 12 conditions. Mean normative cue-target strength: 42% for strong cues, 1% for weak cues. Study 3 s per item or pair, 5 min to write recall. Cued conditions pooled over List A (14.03 words) and List B (13.03).
limits: N per cell not extracted from the text. Lenient scoring (word credited even if written next to the wrong cue).
agent_relevance: Defines the vocabulary: input cue, output cue, match. A cue is only as good as what was stored with the item.

source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: Strong cues given at test helped only if the item was studied alone or with those strong cues.
numbers: Exp I mean words recalled: strong cue at test after no cue at study 19.0 vs 14.1 uncued (O-S vs O-O); strong after strong 20.2 vs 12.2 uncued (S-S vs S-O).
limits: Strong-cue gain is reliable only when encoding was compatible with the cue.
agent_relevance: A retrieval aid built from meaning links helps only for items stored in that form.

source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: The core result: weak cues seen at study helped at test, and weak cues NOT seen at study did nothing or hurt.
numbers: Exp I: weak cue at study and test (W-W) 15.7 vs 10.7 uncued (W-O). Weak cue at test but not at study: 11.1 vs 14.1 (O-W vs O-O) and 9.2 vs 12.2 (S-W vs S-O).
quote: Recall of the TBR words in presence of these cues was greatly facilitated in comparison with noncued recall
limits: Weak cues not shown at study gave scores at or below uncued recall.
agent_relevance: A cue absent from the writing-time record is worth zero or less, even if it is semantically related.

source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: The critical cell: weak cue at study, strong associate (not seen) at test. In Exp I the strong cue helped a little. The authors suspected subjects had not encoded specifically, so Exp II forced specific encoding by repeated matched testing.
numbers: Exp I: W-S 13.9 vs W-O 10.7, but far below S-S 20.2 and O-S 19.0. Exp II (six groups, four lists): groups trained on weak-cue matched tests recalled 18.3 on lists 1-2; an unexpected uncued test on list 3 gave 7.1; the switch to strong cues gave no gain. Groups trained uncued recalled 11.0; unexpected strong-cue test gave 16.8 and 16.3, weak-cue test 10.3.
limits: Exp II: statistics for the strong-cue switch in the weak-trained groups not extracted. Exp I result alone did not match the strict reading of the principle.
agent_relevance: Method trick: repeat matched testing to fix the stored format. Relevant to how an agent writes memory notes.

source: Thomson & Tulving (1970) Associative encoding and retrieval: weak and strong cues
finding: Exp III (mixed list, 24 participants): a strong cue at test hurt when the item had been stored with a weak cue, and a weak cue at test failed for items stored with a strong cue.
numbers: Exp III proportions recalled: weak-input weak-test 0.73 vs weak-input strong-test 0.33 (8 of 24, close to uncued level). Strong-input weak-test about 0.03; only 5 of 24 participants recalled one word.
limits: Mixed lists only; N=24. Strong-to-weak switch was near floor.
agent_relevance: A cue mismatch can cost as much as no cue. Retrieval keys should come from what was stored, not from what seems related.

source: Thomson (1984) Citation Classic commentary on Thomson & Tulving (1970)
finding: The author says he set out to refute Tulving, ran the studies, and the data supported the encoding specificity principle. The reception had two phases: first disputed, then dismissed as obvious.
numbers: Cited in over 170 publications by 1984 (SCI and SSCI).
quote: The effectiveness of a retrieval cue varies directly with the extent it matches the format of the to-be-remembered information
limits: Personal recollection, not data.
agent_relevance: The first test was hostile; the result did not depend on the proposer. A model for our own adversarial checks.

source: Tulving & Osler (1968) Effectiveness of retrieval cues in memory for words
finding: Paywalled; not read. As described in Thomson & Tulving (1970, opened), the 1968 study found that weak cue words presented at study helped recall when reinstated at test and not when absent. The 1970 paper extended the same design.
numbers: No numbers from this source (J Exp Psychol 77(4), 593-601).
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Origin of the cued-recall design. Obtain full text before citing numbers.

source: Tulving & Thomson (1973) Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory
finding: Not opened (no free full text found). Search summaries: participants studied weak cue-target pairs, then were tested with the studied cue or a strong associate that was not studied; the studied weak cue was better. The paper also reported recognition failure of recallable words.
numbers: No numbers read this session (Psychological Review 80, 352-373).
limits: Secondary summary only; the Springer link is a related paper listing, not the 1973 article.
agent_relevance: The principle: what is stored is the target plus its encoding context; retrieval is a match of the cue to that composite.

source: Wikipedia, Recognition failure of recallable words (overview of Tulving & Wiseman 1975)
finding: Recognition can be worse than cued recall for the same item when the cue is the encoded context. The Tulving-Wiseman function describes the dependence between recognition and recall of the same item. The page notes contradictory evidence against basing recognition failure on retrieval failure.
numbers: No numbers on the page text read.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, weak source. Tulving & Wiseman 1975, Watkins & Tulving 1975 and Flexser & Tulving 1978 not opened.
agent_relevance: A yes/no relevance check on a re-shown chunk can fail where a cue-driven recall works. Do not trust a recognition-style check alone.

source: Murre (2021) The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication
finding: Preregistered close replication (results-blind in-principle acceptance, Royal Society Open Science) of the diver study failed. 16 divers, 36-word lists, learned dry or wet and recalled dry or wet after 4 min, all four combinations per diver.
numbers: Interaction of learning and recall environment: F=1.999, df 1,60, p=0.163. Main effect of learning environment F=16.2 (p<0.001); recall environment F=0.601 (p=0.440). Land-learned: no difference between land and underwater recall (p=0.47). Underwater-learned: recall was BETTER on land (p<0.01). Same vs different context overall p=0.215.
limits: Differences: 180 cm heated indoor pool vs open cold water at 7 m; all four conditions in one 1.5 h session vs 4 days (more proactive interference); filmed for TV; probably older, less educated sample. Author calls for more replications.
agent_relevance: The most-cited naturalistic proof of the principle was not replicated in the one attempt. Do not base design on global environment match alone.

source: Murre (2021) The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication
finding: The paper gives figures for the original: interaction F=22.0 (p<0.001). The replication author derived eta-squared 0.647 and a lower-bound Cohen d of 2.708, so a 16-diver replication should have had over 99.9% power if that were the true effect.
numbers: Original: F(interaction)=22.0, eta2=0.647, d>=2.71 (replication author's calculation, df2=12).
limits: Derived from the F value by the replication author; original paper not opened. A very large effect from a small sample is a warning sign.
agent_relevance: Do not reason from one striking small-sample win of context match.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 93 effect sizes, environmental context effects are reliable but small, and larger after long retention or when context is the only cue. (Full text read from a copy in the shared scratch folder.)
numbers: Overall weighted d=0.28 (95% CI +-0.05, n=93; heterogeneity QT=242.47, p<.001). Physical reinstatement d=0.28 (n=83). Reinstatement d=0.23 (n=66); interference reduction d=0.68 (n=10); multiple-context d=0.45 (n=7). Free recall d=0.29 (n=52), recognition d=0.27 (n=28), cued recall d=0.25. Retention <5 min d=0.27; 5 min-1 h 0.22; 1 h-1 day 0.28; 1 day-1 week 0.63 (n=6). Different experimenter at test d=0.62 (n=18) vs same experimenter 0.26 (n=60).
limits: Published studies only; heterogeneous (QT significant); based on studies before video-context methods. One reading says 20% of the 93 effects exceeded d=0.80.
agent_relevance: The average effect of being in the same room is small. Effects grow when context is the only cue available.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis
finding: Two boundary conditions: overshadowing (strong item-to-item associations at study leave little role for context) and outshining (good non-context cues at test make context redundant). Mental reinstatement of context reduces the physical-context effect.
numbers: Associative processing at input d=0.13 (n=29) vs nonassociative d=0.33 (n=12) vs unsure d=0.38 (n=42). Mental reinstatement: 10 effect sizes.
limits: Moderator contrasts across studies, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Outshining: when a good cue is present, extra context adds little. Context cues matter only when other cues are missing.

source: Higham (2002) Strong cues are not necessarily weak: Thomson and Tulving (1970) and the encoding specificity principle revisited
finding: Replication of Thomson & Tulving (1970) with a two-stage test that separates retrieval, monitoring and report bias. Free-report data replicate the old pattern, but with output forced, strong cues also help. Part of the old effect is a reporting effect. (Read from a copy in the shared scratch folder; the DOI is from memory, check it.)
numbers: 48 undergraduates, 100 trials (94 valid). Free-report retrieval: weak cue .24 (trial group) and .29 (phase group) vs no-cue .08 (p<.001 each); strong cues did not beat no-cue (F<1). Forced report: both strong and weak cues far better than no cue. Strong-cue report criterion more conservative than weak-cue.
limits: Strong cues still not shown to match weak cues in free report; monitoring was poor for strong cues. Exact forced-report values not extracted.
agent_relevance: The strong cue is not useless; part of the result is withheld answers. For an agent: force an answer and score it, then decide separately whether to trust it.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle
finding: Four experiments argue that match is not the causal factor. Adding a study cue at test slowed retrieval when the cue was shared by several targets (low diagnostic value). Adding a second unique cue changed nothing.
numbers: Exp 1: accuracy above 90% in all conditions; one-unique-plus-one-shared slower than one-unique (t(24)=2.77, p<.02, one-tailed) and two-unique (t(24)=2.46, p<.03). Exp 1: 27 participants, 24 met criterion. Exp 2 (words): cue-type effect F(2,44)=3.35 on accuracy, F(2,44)=5.18 on RT (p<.01).
limits: Cued recognition with response time as the measure; accuracy near ceiling by design; participants learned to criterion first.
agent_relevance: Cue rule for the agent: a key must point at one thing. Adding matching but non-unique keys slows or confuses.

source: Smith, Handy, Angello & Manzano (2014) Effects of similarity on environmental context cueing
finding: Video contexts give large context effects under favourable conditions: one target per context, intentional item-context encoding, free recall. A never-seen video of the same kind of place still cues recall, less than the original. Labels incompatible with the test video lowered the benefit.
numbers: Three experiments plus a fourth with incidental encoding showing a robust effect on paired associates. Exact effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Lab video method; global-room manipulations give d about .28 per the earlier meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: A similar-but-new cue works partly: cue similarity to the stored context is a gradient. This favours vector retrieval over exact string match.

source: Smith & Manzano (2010) Video context-dependent recall
finding: Reinstating a video context gave very large recall gains, but the gains shrank as more words shared one context (cue overload).
numbers: Exp 1: reinstatement F(1,318)=648.19, eta2=.67. Context load (1, 3, 15 words/context) F(2,318)=27.02, eta2=.15; interaction with reinstatement F(2,318)=60.77, eta2=.28. Reinstatement significant at every load: t(108)=7.24 (15 words), 14.47 (3 words), 21.87 (1 word).
limits: Videos with superimposed words; load varied between subjects. Links to the cue-overload subfield (04).
agent_relevance: A cue shared by many items loses power fast. Index memory so each cue points to few items.

source: Smith & Handy (2014) Effects of varied and constant environmental contexts on acquisition and retention
finding: Four experiments on when memories become free of their context. Retrieval practice with the original video context (constant) or a new context each trial (varied) was compared on later recall without any video.
numbers: Face-name pairs; 5 practice trials; final recall without video. Outcome of the varied-vs-constant contrast not extracted this session.
limits: Abstract-level reading of the design only.
agent_relevance: Varying retrieval conditions during practice is the candidate way to make memory cue-independent; a design lever for agent self-training of notes.

source: Saufley, Otaka & Bavaresco (1985) Context effects: Classroom tests and context independence
finding: Field test in real college classes found no context effect. Students tested in a different room did not score lower.
numbers: No reliable effects in 21 comparisons across seven courses.
limits: Authors say classes induce decontextualisation. Not a lab test of one list.
agent_relevance: Real-world use across varied settings makes items cue-independent. Items used many times in varied settings need no context cue.

source: Hintzman (1986) Schema abstraction in a multiple-trace memory model (MINERVA 2)
finding: MINERVA 2 stores one trace per experience. A cue contacts all traces in parallel, each activated by similarity to the cue; the output is the summed content of the activated traces. General concepts come out of the episodic pool at retrieval.
numbers: Simulation model; no human data here.
quote: A retrieval cue contacts all traces simultaneously, activating each according to its similarity to the cue
limits: Paper is on schema abstraction, not encoding specificity directly; the cue-similarity rule is the formal home of the principle.
agent_relevance: A vector memory with similarity retrieval is MINERVA-like; the stored form is what is matched.

source: Raaijmakers & Shiffrin (1981) Search of associative memory (SAM)
finding: PDF could not be parsed (damaged). Search summaries: SAM treats recall as sampling memory images by match to cues and context, then recovery. Context is a cue like any other.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Formal precedent for putting where/when into the retrieval cue.

source: Howard & Kahana (2002) A distributed representation of temporal context
finding: The temporal context model (TCM): context drifts over time, and each retrieved item reinstates its earlier context state, which then acts as an asymmetric retrieval cue. This explains recency, contiguity and the forward advantage in free recall.
numbers: Modelled single-trial free recall data; no new human experiment in the part read.
limits: Fits free recall; the link to semantic-cue encoding specificity is indirect.
agent_relevance: Store a running context vector with each item so retrieving A also brings back what surrounded it.

source: Morris, Bransford & Franks (1977) Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing
finding: Not opened. Search summaries: semantic encoding beat rhyme encoding on a standard recognition test but the pattern reversed on a rhyming test. Memory depends on whether encoding processes fit the retrieval task.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Secondary only; the URL is a search hit that may be a different article.
agent_relevance: Companion account: match of processes, not only cues. Tests for the agent should resemble the use case.

source: Stern & Nadel (2026) Drawing on Memory: Dual-Trace Encoding Improves Cross-Session Recall in LLM Agents
finding: Each stored fact is paired with a concrete scene trace (when, where, context). On LongMemEval-S, over 99 paired questions, dual-trace beat a fact-only control. The authors invoke encoding specificity.
numbers: 73.7% vs 53.5% overall (+20.2 pp, 95% CI +12.1 to +29.3, bootstrap p<0.0001). Gains: temporal reasoning +40 pp, knowledge update +25 pp, multi-session aggregation +30 pp; single-session fact retrieval 75% vs 75%. Vanilla Letta agent 20.0%. Session coverage 54.8% vs 57.4%. Tokens per query 3.3% lower for dual-trace.
limits: One benchmark, 20 questions per type, one run; the ablation that would separate scene-at-encoding from scene-at-retrieval was not run. Preprint. Not a direct test of the encoding-retrieval match.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the memory layer: store a context scene with each fact. The effect is on questions about time and updates, not on simple lookup.

source: Stern & Nadel (2026) Drawing on Memory: Dual-Trace Encoding Improves Cross-Session Recall in LLM Agents
finding: Ladder of earlier conditions: flat storage changes alone added little; the scene step added the largest jump.
numbers: C1 to C5 about 40.4% to 48.5%; C5 to C7 (coverage and format) +5 pp to 53.5%; C7 to C6 (scene traces) +20.2 pp. Abstention accuracy 100% vs 95% (p=0.351).
limits: Same single-benchmark limits.
agent_relevance: Encoding distinctiveness mattered more than coverage in this test.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu & Thilakarathna (2026) Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from the Encoding Specificity Principle
finding: Attention is read as cue-based retrieval: queries are the retrieval context, keys index traces, values carry content. Swapping keys and values for counterfactual ones changes what the model recalls.
numbers: Swapping V only: clean replacement of knowledge. Swapping K and V: 100% hallucination of the factual prompts in all models tested. Swapping K only: factual accuracy about 30-40%. Counterfactual replacement 50% (Olmo-2) to 90% (Qwen2.5).
limits: Open models only; keywords come from GPT-4o and the paper's neuron analysis; the Tulving link is an analogy; authors admit top-neuron choices are arbitrary.
agent_relevance: Keys decide what is fetched inside the model; surface keywords in a prompt can act as cues. Read cautiously.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu & Thilakarathna (2026) Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from the Encoding Specificity Principle
finding: Keywords-as-cues test: zeroing key projections for identified keywords cut recall of memorised text more than zeroing random tokens. In Olmo 2 13B, perturbing keywords in all attention heads sharply reduced ROUGE-L recall and BERTScore while random tokens had minimal effect.
numbers: ROUGE-L recall and BERTScore on book text; Llama-2 7B and 13B showed almost no difference between the three keyword-extraction methods (authors blame the 32,000-token vocabulary).
limits: Memorised book text, not episodic memory of new items. Causal claim limited to attention-key perturbation.
agent_relevance: Salient lexical tokens act as cues: keep the exact words a later query will use when writing notes.

source: Wikipedia, Context-dependent memory
finding: The page says context effects are larger in recall than in recognition (citing Godden & Baddeley 1980). The Smith & Vela meta-analysis gives free recall d=.29 and recognition d=.27, a small difference.
numbers: Meta-analytic: free recall .29, recognition .27, cued recall .25.
limits: Wikipedia is a weak source; the two statements differ in size and come from different paradigms.
agent_relevance: Do not assume recognition-style checks are immune to context effects.
